paragraphs: Stochastic approximation updates an estimate using noisy information arriving over time. Producing an estimate is only part of the statistical problem: researchers also need confidence intervals that express its uncertainty. This paper develops an online inference framework for a class of these procedures with a constant step size, including stochastic gradient descent and Q-learning.

The authors treat the sequence of updates as a time-homogeneous Markov chain, meaning that the rule governing transitions stays fixed over time. They establish a functional central limit theorem under weaker conditions and provide an alternative condition suited to stochastic approximation. This theorem describes the large-scale fluctuations of the update process and supplies the basis for statistical inference.

The framework constructs confidence intervals through random scaling, using the observed stochastic process to scale uncertainty. In the reported experiments, this approach gives more accurate and robust inference than the traditional methods considered. The contribution connects constant-step optimization and learning procedures with a principled way to quantify uncertainty while those procedures operate.
neurips-2022-a-statistical-online-infere.tldr: A Markov-chain framework enables online confidence intervals for constant-step stochastic approximation, with random scaling improving inference in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Optimization algorithms depend on choices such as learning rates and how updates are rescaled across parameter directions. Amortized Proximal Optimization, or APO, learns these choices during optimization. Its starting point is an interpretation of existing neural network optimizers as approximate proximal methods: each update balances reducing the current batch loss against changing the weights and the function represented by the network.

APO trains the parameters of an update rule to reduce this proximal objective. The learned rule spreads the work of solving that objective across optimization steps. It can adapt either a learning rate or a structured preconditioning matrix. Under appropriate assumptions, the framework recovers established approaches including natural gradient descent and KFAC.

Experiments cover regression, image reconstruction, classification, and translation. Learned learning-rate schedules generally outperform optimal fixed rates and compete with manually tuned decay schedules; learned preconditioners generally compete with second-order methods. APO also avoids matrix inversion, keeping overhead low and improving numerical stability. The authors identify this stability as useful for training with low-precision arithmetic.
neurips-2022-amortized-proximal-optimiza.tldr: APO learns optimizer settings online through a proximal objective, achieving competitive optimization without matrix inverses.

paragraphs: A defense against adversarial manipulation should withstand attacks that account for how the defense works. This paper argues that evaluations of graph neural network defenses have generally missed that requirement. Testing with non-adaptive attacks can make a defense appear stronger because the attack does not specifically challenge the protection being evaluated.

The authors analyze seven popular defenses covering changes to the graph, the network architecture, and the training procedure. They design adaptive attacks for these defenses and examine robustness under those attacks. Most evaluated defenses offer no improvement, or only marginal improvement, over an undefended baseline. This challenges the apparent progress suggested by the earlier evaluation methodology.

The paper recommends custom adaptive attacks as the standard for evaluating robustness and shares lessons from constructing them. It also provides a diverse collection of perturbed graphs that can serve as a black-box unit test. That collection offers an initial robustness check, while the broader finding emphasizes the importance of testing a defense against attacks tailored to it.
neurips-2022-are-defenses-for-graph-neur.tldr: Adaptive attacks reveal that most of seven evaluated graph neural network defenses provide little or no robustness improvement.

paragraphs: Generative adversarial models try to make generated data difficult to distinguish from real data, whereas likelihood-based models learn to assign high probability to observed examples. This paper investigates why likelihood methods have been more widely successful for sequential generation, especially text. It asks how different these two objectives really are when model capacity is taken into account.

For a broad class of adversarial objectives, the authors argue that much of the apparent distinction comes from the limited expressiveness of the model family. They develop a theoretical setting in which minimizing KL divergence, corresponding to maximizing likelihood, more efficiently reduces the distinguishability criteria targeted by adversarial training.

The analysis gives reductions relating distinguishability minimization to improving likelihood for model families including n-grams and neural networks with softmax outputs. A next-token distinguishability formulation enables a full polynomial-time reduction. Preliminary empirical evidence supports the theoretical account. These results offer a qualified explanation for likelihood training's effectiveness on sequential data, rather than establishing that adversarial modeling is unnecessary for every generation problem.
neurips-2022-are-gans-overkill-for-nlp-c.tldr: The paper gives theoretical settings where likelihood training efficiently achieves distinguishability objectives associated with adversarial text generation.

paragraphs: Weak supervision creates training labels by combining inexpensive, imperfect labeling rules. Writing those rules becomes difficult when inputs have complex or high-dimensional features. Automated weak supervision tries to construct the rules from a small collection of trusted labels, potentially making the approach usable in domains where manual rule design has been impractical.

AutoWS-Bench-101 evaluates this strategy across diverse, challenging application domains. Its central comparison starts each task with 100 labels and asks how practitioners should use them. One option is to generate more labels through automated weak supervision; alternatives include supervised learning with the available labels or zero-shot predictions from a foundation model.

In the benchmark's observations, automated weak supervision needs information from foundation models to outperform simple few-shot baselines. This identifies an empirical requirement in the evaluated settings, rather than a universal rule for every application. The framework and accompanying ablation study help examine whether automated labeling adds value and how it can cooperate with modern foundation-model capabilities.
neurips-2022-autows-bench-101-benchmarki.tldr: AutoWS-Bench-101 tests how best to use 100 labels and finds foundation-model signals necessary for AutoWS to beat simple few-shot baselines in its evaluations.

paragraphs: Safe reinforcement learning asks an agent to improve its reward while respecting safety constraints. These goals must be considered together when updating the agent's policy, the rule that determines its actions. This paper introduces Constrained Update Projection, or CUP, as a policy optimization framework with a rigorous safety guarantee.

CUP is built around new surrogate functions and a performance bound. The surrogate functions support generalized advantage estimation, which supplies estimates used to guide policy improvement. The framework also unifies performance bounds, helping interpret some existing algorithms within a shared analysis. These theoretical elements connect the practical update procedure to claims about its behavior.

The implementation handles non-convex optimization using only first-order optimizers and does not require a strong approximation that makes the objectives convex. This makes the optimization procedure a central part of the contribution alongside the analysis. Across a wide range of tasks and safe reinforcement-learning baselines, the reported experiments show effectiveness in both reward and satisfaction of safety constraints.
neurips-2022-constrained-update-projecti.tldr: CUP combines theoretically grounded safety constraints with first-order policy optimization and shows effective reward and constraint satisfaction in experiments.

paragraphs: An agent may lack the capacity to learn every detail of its environment, even when it needs a model for planning. Value equivalence offers a way to focus on details relevant to evaluating behavior. This paper considers the harder situation in which the agent cannot even represent an exactly value-equivalent model and must accept some loss in decision quality.

The proposed algorithm uses rate-distortion theory to construct an approximately value-equivalent compression of the environment. It repeatedly selects a simplified model that balances how much information must be learned against the resulting sub-optimality. This makes the choice of what to model part of the learning problem itself.

The authors prove an information-theoretic Bayesian regret bound for finite-horizon, episodic sequential decision problems. The guarantee can be expressed in two ways: finding the simplest model compatible with a desired sub-optimality gap, or finding the best model under a capacity limit. These formulations give complementary accounts of the same tradeoff between limited representation and effective decisions.
neurips-2022-deciding-what-to-model-valu.tldr: A rate-distortion algorithm trades environment-model complexity against decision quality, with Bayesian regret guarantees for finite-horizon episodic problems.

paragraphs: Open-world detection seeks to locate objects described by arbitrary category names. DetCLIP addresses this by combining visual learning with a dictionary of concepts and their descriptions. Its motivation includes an inefficiency in GLIP's formulation, which joins detection category names into sentences and thereby introduces interactions among those names.

DetCLIP processes concepts separately, allowing training to draw on detection data, grounding data, and image-text pairs. The concept dictionary supplies descriptive prior knowledge and explicitly connects related concepts. It also provides negative concepts for learning which words match which image regions, and helps complete labels for objects omitted from image captions.

The reported zero-shot results show that this combination improves detection in the evaluated setting. On LVIS, DetCLIP-T exceeds GLIP-T by 9.9% mAP and reports a 13.5% improvement on rare categories over a fully supervised model with the same backbone. These findings support using structured concept descriptions and heterogeneous training data to improve recognition beyond a fixed category vocabulary.
neurips-2022-detclip-dictionary-enriched.tldr: DetCLIP combines separately processed visual concepts with a descriptive dictionary to improve zero-shot object detection.

paragraphs: Physical systems with many interacting bodies can contain meaningful structure at several scales. Conventional equivariant graph networks exchange information on a flat graph, limiting their ability to discover substructures and combine information globally. This paper introduces a hierarchy so that the model can connect detailed dynamics with the behavior of larger groups.

The architecture has three main components. Equivariant Matrix Message Passing increases the expressiveness of the information exchanged between nodes. E-Pool assigns quantities from lower-level nodes to higher-level clusters. E-UnPool then uses information from those clusters to update the dynamics of the original nodes, allowing information to travel up and back down the hierarchy.

Both pooling operations are guaranteed to preserve equivariance, maintaining the required correspondence between physical symmetries and model outputs. The authors evaluate the resulting networks on multi-object simulation, motion capture, and protein dynamics. The experiments support the usefulness of combining hierarchical information flow with symmetry-respecting operations across these applications, where local interactions and larger-scale organization both matter.
neurips-2022-equivariant-graph-hierarchy.tldr: Equivariant hierarchical graph networks combine local dynamics and cluster-level information while preserving physical symmetry.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly stochastic gradient descent with weight decay approaches an equilibrium distribution when the loss is scale invariant, as can occur with normalization schemes. The relevant notion of mixing concerns the functions represented by the network. The question is how quickly their distribution settles, rather than whether one parameter vector stops moving.

The authors prove the Fast Equilibrium Conjecture under two assumptions: the noise covariance is non-degenerate, and the loss minimizers form a connected, compact, analytic manifold. Under these conditions, the mixing time is approximately inverse in the product of learning rate and weight decay, up to the factors suppressed by the stated asymptotic notation.

The analysis also derives a limiting stochastic differential equation as that product approaches zero, with the learning rate constrained relative to weight decay. Its distribution approaches the same equilibrium for every initialization around the minimizer manifold as limiting time grows. The result therefore gives a conditional explanation of how normalization, noise, and weight decay can lead different nearby initializations toward a shared distribution of functions.
neurips-2022-fast-mixing-of-stochastic-g.tldr: Under stated noise and minimizer-geometry assumptions, SGD on scale-invariant losses mixes in function space at a rate governed by learning rate times weight decay.

paragraphs: Kernel matrix-vector multiplication is a basic operation in machine learning and scientific computing, but its time and memory demands can grow quadratically with the number of points. The Faster-Fast and Free Memory Method, abbreviated F³M, approximates this operation for exceptionally large datasets with relatively few features: roughly one hundred million to one billion points, with dimension at most seven.

The reported experiments show empirical linear growth in time and memory, with relative error on the order of one thousandth. On a high-end GPU, the method performs a full approximate multiplication for a billion points in under a minute. These are experimental scaling and accuracy results for the targeted low-dimensional setting.

The authors also test whether the approximation helps complete learning systems. Used inside the GPU solver FALKON, it provides speedups of 1.5 to 5.5 times with less than a 1% accuracy drop. Gaussian process regression experiments show competitive results with substantial speedups, supporting the method's usefulness beyond an isolated computational benchmark.
neurips-2022-giga-scale-kernel-matrix-ve.tldr: F³M approximates kernel matrix-vector products at billion-point scale on GPUs, showing empirical linear scaling for low-dimensional data.

paragraphs: The order in which training examples are processed can affect optimization. Random reshuffling selects a new permutation each epoch, while greedy ordering methods can improve convergence empirically but require substantial resources. This paper develops a theoretically justified ordering framework called herding and then makes its benefits more practical through Gradient Balancing, or GraB.

For smooth, non-convex objectives, the authors establish a convergence rate of O(T^(-2/3)) for SGD with herding, compared with O(n^(1/3)T^(-2/3)) for random reshuffling. Here n counts examples and T counts iterations. The improvement removes the displayed dependence on dataset size while retaining the same iteration exponent.

GraB uses discrepancy minimization to achieve the same rate with an online procedure. It reduces memory from O(nd) to O(d), where d is model dimension, and computation from O(n²) to O(n). Experiments across image and language tasks show that GraB can improve training and validation performance over random reshuffling and outperform greedy ordering while using over 100 times less memory.
neurips-2022-grab-finding-provably-bette.tldr: GraB balances gradients to choose data orders with a stronger convergence rate than random reshuffling and much lower overhead than greedy ordering.

paragraphs: Large vision transformers can be expensive to run on devices such as phones and watches. Knowledge distillation addresses this by training a compact student using information from a larger teacher. This paper argues that approaches designed around convolutional networks do not fully exploit a distinctive source of information in transformers: their image patches.

The proposed method trains a tiny student to match a pretrained teacher in a patch-level manifold space. The transfer therefore uses structure in patch representations and their relationships. To reduce the cost of computing those relationships, the authors split the manifold-matching objective into three carefully designed terms.

With this method, a DeiT-Tiny model containing five million parameters reaches 76.5% top-1 accuracy on ImageNet-1k, reported as a 2.0% improvement over previous distillation approaches. Transfer experiments on other classification benchmarks and downstream vision tasks also favor the method over the compared approaches. The findings support patch-level representation structure as a useful teaching signal for compact vision transformers.
neurips-2022-learning-efficient-vision-t.tldr: Matching a teacher's patch-level representation structure improves compact vision transformers, with DeiT-Tiny reaching 76.5% ImageNet-1k top-1 accuracy.

paragraphs: When training examples are scarce, incorporating knowledge about the problem can be valuable. This paper brings several properties associated with convolutional neural networks into support-vector machines. A central example is transformation invariance: images related by a relevant transformation, such as translation, should retain an appropriate notion of similarity.

The proposed kernels use the maximum similarity over a group of transformations. Such kernels are not generally positive definite, a mathematical property important to the kernel formulation. The authors show that positive definiteness holds with high probability in the small-training-sample regime they study. The qualification matters: the result does not establish positive definiteness for arbitrary datasets.

The paper also incorporates local features at multiple spatial scales and composition through multiple layers into the SVM approach. Experiments on available image datasets show superior accuracy over established deep neural network benchmarks when sample sizes are small. Together, the theory and experiments support building relevant invariances and multiscale structure directly into models intended for limited-data learning.
neurips-2022-learning-from-few-samples-t.tldr: Transformation-aware, multiscale SVMs outperform tested deep-network benchmarks with few samples, with a qualified positive-definiteness result for their kernels.

paragraphs: Predicting interacting objects requires learning both how each object behaves independently and how other objects influence it. This paper develops a continuous-time model that separates those contributions while estimating uncertainty. Its latent Gaussian process ordinary differential equations represent the dynamics in a way intended to support reliable predictions beyond the observed trajectories.

Each object becomes a node in a graph, and neighboring objects contribute messages that are accumulated to represent interactions. Separate functions capture independent dynamics and interaction effects. The authors use variational sparse Gaussian process inference to make learning feasible despite the complex network of dependent variables.

In the reported experiments, the model improves the reliability of long-term predictions compared with neural-network alternatives and handles missing dynamic or static information. Among the compared models, it alone successfully separates independent behavior and interactions into distinct functions. The authors also demonstrate benefits from this separation in extrapolation scenarios, connecting the model's internal organization to its ability to predict outside the observed setting.
neurips-2022-learning-interacting-dynami.tldr: Latent Gaussian process ODEs separate individual dynamics from interactions and improve uncertainty-aware long-term prediction in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Understanding an indoor scene involves identifying both whole objects and their movable parts. MultiScan provides a pipeline and dataset for studying that richer form of 3D understanding. The pipeline uses commodity mobile devices to capture RGBD data, combining color and depth, and web interfaces to annotate objects, parts, and parameters describing part mobility.

The resulting dataset contains 230 scans of 108 indoor scenes, covering 9,458 objects and 4,331 parts. It includes RGBD streams, camera poses for individual frames, textured surface meshes, and semantic labels at both object and part levels. Mobility parameters add information about how parts can move, extending the data beyond static object identity and shape.

The authors evaluate the dataset through instance segmentation and part mobility estimation, benchmarking methods from prior work. Their experiments show that segmenting parts and estimating mobility in real scenes remain difficult despite progress in whole-object segmentation. MultiScan therefore supplies both a practical collection process and a benchmark for studying these unresolved aspects of scene understanding.
neurips-2022-multiscan-scalable-rgbd-sca.tldr: MultiScan pairs scalable mobile 3D scanning with object, part, and mobility annotations, exposing continuing challenges in understanding movable scene parts.

paragraphs: Controllers for physical systems must often stabilize behavior despite randomness. This paper develops neural controllers for stochastic systems, where a control policy must account for uncertain dynamics as it steers the system toward a target. The authors propose two approaches with different stability guarantees and different training costs.

The exponential stabilizer uses stochastic Lyapunov theory and can make the controlled system converge exponentially. Its drawback is a long computational time. The asymptotic stabilizer uses stochastic asymptotic stability theory and trains much faster, but guarantees only asymptotic attractiveness of the target, without the exponential convergence guarantee. The two methods therefore offer complementary choices.

The authors also analyze linear control rigorously in terms of convergence time and energy cost, then compare it numerically with their neural controllers on those dimensions. Examples involving representative physical systems demonstrate the proposed controllers' usefulness for stabilization. The central finding is a concrete tradeoff between the strength of the convergence guarantee and the computational effort required to train a stochastic controller.
neurips-2022-neural-stochastic-control-b.tldr: Two neural stochastic controllers trade slower training with exponential convergence against faster training with an asymptotic stability guarantee.

paragraphs: Evaluating a decision policy becomes difficult when the environment changes over time. Those changes may arise from external forces, from the agent's own actions, or from both. This paper studies on-policy and off-policy evaluation under these forms of non-stationarity, with the goal of predicting a policy's future performance from past information.

The key assumption is higher-order stationarity: the environment can change, but the mechanism describing how it changes stays fixed. This supplies structure that an evaluation algorithm can learn. The proposed method, OPEN, applies counterfactual reasoning twice and combines it with importance-weighted instrumental-variable regression to estimate patterns in the policy's past performance.

The authors describe this construction as yielding lower bias and lower variance when estimating the structure of performance changes. Experiments in several domains inspired by real applications give promising results for forecasting future policy performance. The contribution depends on stable structure in the change process, making that assumption central to how OPEN addresses environments whose ordinary decision dynamics are not stationary.
neurips-2022-off-policy-evaluation-for-a.tldr: OPEN estimates future policy performance in changing environments by assuming that the mechanism governing change remains stable.

paragraphs: Eye care draws on several kinds of information, including images, biomarkers, clinical measurements, and treatment history. OLIVES brings these sources together so researchers can study their relationships over time. It focuses on data associated with diabetic retinopathy and diabetic macular edema, linking imaging to labels and treatment information from clinical trials.

The dataset contains 1,268 near-infrared fundus images, each associated with at least 49 OCT scans. It also includes 16 biomarkers, four clinical labels, and a disease diagnosis. Data cover 96 eyes, with an average observation period of at least two years; treatment averages are 66 weeks and seven injections per eye.

This organization supports research into how different measurements relate across a treatment period, rather than treating each image as an isolated example. The authors benchmark the dataset's utility for ophthalmic analysis and provide benchmarks and research directions for machine learning in medical imaging. The contribution is a connected, longitudinal research resource, with imaging and clinical context available together.
neurips-2022-olives-dataset-ophthalmic-l.tldr: OLIVES links longitudinal eye imaging with biomarkers, clinical labels, diagnoses, and treatment histories for multimodal medical-image research.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a vision transformer's computation by removing parts of the network. SAViT argues that deciding what to remove independently within each component overlooks interactions between components with different roles. It introduces joint importance, which evaluates those structural relationships so that pruning decisions can be coordinated across the model.

The method uses a Taylor-based approximation, motivated by theoretical analysis, to estimate joint importance. This encourages a more balanced reduction across components. Under mild assumptions, the authors further incorporate component interactions into the optimization objective to lower the algorithm's complexity. The approach can also be applied to tasks such as object detection.

On ImageNet, the reported result improves accuracy by 0.7% over the DeiT-Base baseline while reducing FLOPs by 50%. On COCO, it removes 70% of FLOPs from FasterRCNN with a ViT backbone with a 0.3% mAP drop. These findings support accounting for interactions when allocating a model's reduced computation budget, rather than judging every component in isolation.
neurips-2022-savit-structure-aware-visio.tldr: SAViT coordinates pruning across interacting transformer components, substantially reducing computation while preserving or improving reported task performance.

paragraphs: SoundSpaces 2.0 generates audio from the geometry of a 3D environment while a simulation runs. Given a mesh of a real space, it can render sounds as captured at arbitrary microphone locations. Combined with visual assets, this provides a shared setting for studying systems that use both sight and hearing.

The platform supports continuous choices of spatial position, use in previously unseen environments, and configurable microphone and material properties. These capabilities make it useful for tasks including navigation, mapping, sound-source localization, source separation, and acoustic matching. The authors emphasize the combination of realistic geometry-based acoustics and sufficient speed for embodied learning.

The evaluation compares simulated acoustics against real-world audio measurements and demonstrates embodied navigation and far-field speech recognition. For speech recognition, the paper highlights transfer from simulation to the real world. The publicly available platform therefore contributes both an acoustic rendering resource and evidence that it can support downstream learning, including a reported application beyond the simulated setting.
neurips-2022-soundspaces-2-0-a-simulatio.tldr: SoundSpaces 2.0 renders realistic audio in 3D environments fast enough for embodied learning and demonstrates simulation-to-real transfer for speech recognition.

paragraphs: This paper asks how restrictions on neural-network weights affect the amount of data needed for uniform convergence guarantees. Such guarantees control the gap between sample behavior and population behavior across a class of networks. The main setting is scalar-output networks with one hidden layer and inputs bounded in Euclidean norm.

The authors show that controlling the spectral norm of the hidden-layer weight matrix is generally insufficient for guarantees independent of network width. A stronger Frobenius norm restriction is sufficient. This separates two common ways of limiting weight magnitude and shows that the choice of constraint can materially change what a width-independent guarantee can establish.

The paper then identifies settings where spectral norm control does suffice: sufficiently smooth activation functions, with an extension to deeper networks, and certain convolutional architectures. For the convolutional case, it also examines how patch overlap and patch count affect sample complexity. The results make architecture and activation regularity central to deciding when a weaker norm restriction can support the desired guarantee.
neurips-2022-the-sample-complexity-of-on.tldr: Spectral norm control alone generally fails to give width-independent uniform convergence, but suffices under particular smoothness or convolutional-architecture conditions.

paragraphs: Forecasting several related time series requires understanding how their relationships evolve. The paper argues that common graph neural networks emphasize pairwise connections and often overlook time-dependent topology. Its proposed architecture, ZFC-SHCN, combines temporal structural information with interactions involving more than two nodes.

The first component is a computationally efficient zigzag persistence curve that encodes topological information conditioned on time. The second is a temporal multiplex graph module that learns higher-order interactions. Together, they extend simplicial neural-network ideas with a representation of changing structure, allowing forecasting to use both group relationships and their temporal organization.

The authors discuss theoretical properties of the representation and evaluate the model on synthetic and real data, including traffic, COVID-19 biosurveillance, Ethereum, temperature, wind energy, and vector autoregressions. The experiments report state-of-the-art forecasting performance with lower computational requirements. These findings support the proposed combination in the tested settings: temporal topology and higher-order interactions can provide useful predictive structure without requiring greater computation than the compared approaches.
neurips-2022-time-conditioned-dances-wit.tldr: ZFC-SHCN combines time-dependent topology and higher-order interactions, reporting improved time-series forecasting with lower computational costs.

paragraphs: Understanding a classifier can require more than inspecting its final features or a single intermediate layer. Coded ResNeXt makes the network's organization itself more transparent by assigning class-relevant information to specific paths. These paths are planned before training using coding theory, without relying on semantic similarities between the classes.

Each path can operate independently as a model with a single purpose. For any class, the architecture therefore yields a binary classifier without additional training, using at least 60% fewer parameters than the original network. The coding-based design also permits predictions at intermediate layers, so inference can produce an early prediction without evaluating the entire model.

The authors demonstrate these properties with a slightly modified ResNeXt on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet-1k. They also report improved overall accuracy alongside the architectural capabilities. The contribution links transparency to practical reuse: class-specific paths provide a way to inspect how information is organized, extract smaller classifiers, and make intermediate predictions within the same trained network.
neurips-2022-towards-disentangling-infor.tldr: Coded ResNeXt assigns classes predefined information paths that support smaller standalone classifiers and early predictions while improving reported accuracy.

paragraphs: An explanation of why a classifier favors one class may highlight features that also support several other classes. Such an explanation does not necessarily reveal what distinguishes the chosen class from its alternatives. This paper develops explanations around that contrast, asking which features explain the preference for one class over others.

The authors propose a weighted contrastive framework that can convert existing back-propagation explanation methods into class-contrastive versions. It builds comparative information into the explanation rather than focusing solely on a prespecified class. They provide theoretical validation for general back-propagation explanations and report significant improvements in both qualitative and quantitative experiments.

The study also identifies a distinction between explaining predicted logits and explaining predicted probabilities. These are different targets, and the authors argue that explanation work often blurs them. Explicitly identifying which target is being explained helps clarify what the resulting attribution means. The overall contribution combines a practical transformation of explanation methods with a more precise account of the question those explanations answer.
neurips-2022-why-not-other-classes-towar.tldr: A weighted contrastive framework adapts back-propagation explanations to show why a classifier favors one class over alternatives.
